# Independent audit: thin convex measures and common-weight ball lifts



## Single-measure limit and exact exponent

I verified the classification input in the author-uploaded primary text of [Fradelizi–Guédon, Section 2](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220452814_The_Extreme_Points_of_Subsets_of_s_-Concave_Probabilities_and_a_Geometric_Localization_Theorem). Borell's characterization there uses the dimension of the least affine support and gives density exponent \(s/(1-sq)\), with the constant-density endpoint and the Dirac alternative above \(1/q\). With \(s=1/m\), this yields exactly the alternatives and the exponent \(1/(m-q)\) stated in the note.

Brunn–Minkowski is applied inside each original body's own \(m\)-dimensional affine hull, so varying affine hulls cause no missing Jacobian. The weak-closure proof has the correct Portmanteau directions: open neighborhoods provide the lower bounds for the two source masses, and a closed neighborhood of their compact Minkowski sum provides the upper bound for the target limsup. Continuity from above then recovers the desired compact-set inequality. This does not require uniformly bounded original bodies, since weak convergence to a probability is assumed.

The bounded-support and bounded-density arguments are valid. An interior ball on which the positive concave root has a positive lower bound, averaged with distant support points, would give infinitely many disjoint fixed-radius balls of uniformly positive mass. Averaging it with points of arbitrarily large root value would already violate finite mass on one such ball. This justifies compactness and the finite upper semicontinuous concave closure. The uniform-density endpoint has bounded support for the same convex-geometric volume reason.

The ball lift has exactly the stated radius \((f/\kappa_r)^{1/r}\), volume \(\int f\), and projected unnormalized volume law. Thin rescaling contributes the Jacobian \(\epsilon^r\); dividing by its own volume leaves the projected probability unchanged. The Dirac and full-dimensional uniform endpoints are treated separately. In particular the note does not use a nonexistent finite exponent when \(q=m\), and its unit-volume caveat correctly fixes the projection coordinates.

## Independent normalizations versus a common normalization

The three thin rectangles have areas \((\epsilon,2\epsilon,\epsilon)\) and the exact displayed integer fibers. Their separately normalized laws have densities \((1,1/2,1)\) on intervals of lengths \((1,2,1)\). Since \(\kappa_1=2\), their unit-area ball lifts have the stated half-heights \((1/2,1/4,1/2)\), and fail midpoint containment.

The stronger obstruction to **any** equal-volume convex lifts is also correct. Midpoint containment plus equal full-dimensional volumes forces equality in Brunn–Minkowski; the endpoints are translates and the middle is their midpoint body. Their projections must then have equal interval lengths. This contradicts the prescribed supports independently of the chosen hidden dimension or canonical shape.

Under the one common normalizer \(4\epsilon\), all three projected densities instead equal \(1/4\) on their respective supports. The lifted rectangles have common height \(1/4\) and retain the correct masses \((1/4,1/2,1/4)\). The repair preserves relative masses rather than merely replacing all three probability laws by convenient shapes.

## Finite-family compatibility and normalized-limit compactness

For a single fixed orthogonal decomposition and a single common multiplier, section volume is upper semicontinuous for compact convex bodies, including lower-dimensional sections. Its \(r\)-th root is concave. Applying Brunn–Minkowski to the actual nonempty source sections proves every anchored finite ball-radius inequality, including zero-volume sections. The triangle inequality then proves the full set inclusion. Fubini gives both exact mass and projected-law identities. Only caps with zero hidden-coordinate normal are claimed preserved.

In Section 5, positive limiting weights and full-dimensional support in the common \(q\)-projection imply a uniform projection inball: small neighborhoods of affinely independent limit support points carry positive mass and are met by all sufficiently late projections. Their convex hulls contain a fixed smaller ball. At a maximum section radius, averaging with this projection ball gives the stated lower volume bound. Since normalized volume is at most one, the radius cannot escape even when the original total volume tends to zero.

The resulting uniform container gives simultaneous Hausdorff subsequences. Positive limiting volumes rule out dimensional collapse of the lifts. Volume and projected measures converge by indicator convergence off the null boundary of the full-dimensional limit. Hidden rotational symmetry survives; together with the projected density it determines every interior ball section. Closure of the body's interior fixes its boundary, so the subsequential limit is unique. This proves whole-sequence convergence and exact preservation of every anchored inclusion, without an unsupported relative-error estimate.

The note explicitly restricts this positive-limit argument to positive weights. A common projection need not identify the full original laws when their support directions differ. No recovery of discarded transverse cap information or convergence of original mixed depths is inferred.

## Cross-measure Brunn–Minkowski and optimization of radii

Support inclusion follows from positive neighborhoods and the cross-measure inequality. An average of interior source points is interior to the target support, so the concave density representatives are continuous and positive there. The small-ball expansion has precisely the factors \(\kappa_q^{1/m}\epsilon^{q/m}\). Its arbitrary positive radii are essential.

After normalizing \(\sum\lambda_i a_i=1\), the Jensen calculation in (16) is correct with \(b_i=f_i^{1/r}\), \(S=\sum\lambda_i b_i\), and \(\omega_i=\lambda_i b_i/S\). The upper bound \(S^{1-q/m}\) is attained at \(a_i=b_i/S\). Thus optimizing the radius parameters yields the stronger density-root exponent \(1/(m-q)\), rather than the weaker inequality obtained from equal radii.

The boundary set inclusion follows by approximating arbitrary lift points from the full interiors and taking closure. The converse applies ordinary \(m\)-dimensional Brunn–Minkowski to the compact cylinder portions of the lifts; Fubini supplies exactly the original finite measure masses. All finite anchored combinations are included, not only successive integer midpoint operations.

The common-normalized weak-limit passage repeats the correctly oriented neighborhood argument and never interchanges pointwise densities with weak limits. On a finite lattice-convex base family, the anchored inclusions give the exact integer fibers of the convex hull of the lifts. A cap bound on that lifted source transfers to its projection by pulling back containing halfspaces. If an original ambient normal vanishes on the represented support subspace, the containing pullback is the whole space, which satisfies the same bound trivially. This minor degenerate interpretation does not affect the assertion.

## Full-support endpoint \(q=m\)

When the density-root exponent is infinite, the densities are constants \(c_z\) on their convex supports. The linear small-ball inequality forces \(c_j\ge\max_{i:\lambda_i>0}c_{z_i}\), together with the support inclusion. Conversely those conditions give the cross-measure inequality by ordinary Brunn–Minkowski, with the constants retained.

The conditions do not force equal constants. The example with endpoint constants one and middle constant two is valid. The proposed extra height coordinate represents these laws exactly and preserves the anchored inclusions, because the target height dominates the weighted source heights. It increases dimension and is correctly not presented as a free representation in the original dimension.

Thus the note supplies exact common-weight representations under its stated common-support conditions, while explicitly preserving the gaps caused by different affine directions, zero limiting weights, and dimension-dependent depth constants.
